summary: A 1970 note with protocol notes for the ARPA Network. It collects the author's thoughts on ideas being discussed for the network's protocols. It is a discussion paper, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 46 proposes layers for network message delivery, host-level process connections, and remote process creation. It describes possible commands and socket states as a contribution to protocol discussions.

subtitle: A proposed layered design for the ARPA Network's host-to-host protocol.

tldr.problem: The Network Working Group needed an initial host-to-host protocol that sites could implement while leaving room for later extensions.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal separates the IMP network, per-host Network Control Programs (NCPs), and a User Control and Communication (UCC) level for remote process creation.
tldr.outcome: RFC 46 is a proposal for discussion and does not describe a finalized protocol.

today: RFC 46 is listed with status Unknown. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the text presents a proposal for discussion.

sections.title: Three Communication Levels
sections.content:
The proposal divides the network communication system into three levels. The IMP network moves messages between hosts; each host's Network Control Program (NCP) provides communication paths between processes; and the User Control and Communication (UCC) module supports interaction with a foreign host's logger and a created process.

The UCC is one possible third-level protocol. Other applications could implement a different protocol over the NCP system.
sections.plainLanguage: The design separates message transport, connections between host processes, and remote user or process setup. Each level has a different role.

sections.title: Socket Identifiers and States
sections.content:
Processes communicate through simplex connections between send and receive sockets. A socket identifier is 48 bits and includes a user number, an instance tag, a host number, and a socket code.

The proposed socket states are inactive, open, and connected. An event queue records events such as a foreign connection request, acceptance, rejection, or closure.
sections.plainLanguage: Each connection joins a sending socket to a receiving socket. The NCP records whether a socket is inactive, waiting for a connection, or connected.

sections.title: NCP Commands and Data Flow
sections.content:
The proposed NCP control commands include RFC to request a connection, CLS to close one, BLK and RSM to block and resume output, INT to interrupt a process, ERR to report an erroneous command, ECO to test communication, and NOP.

Applications use calls such as LISTEN, INIT, STATUS, ACCEPT, REJECT, CLOSE, INTERRUPT, and TRANSMIT. The RFC describes connection setup as an exchange of requests and acceptance, followed by data transfer subject to flow control.
sections.plainLanguage: The NCP handles connection requests, closure, flow control, and data transfer. Programs use local calls to ask the NCP to listen, connect, accept, or transmit.

sections.title: Creating a Remote Process
sections.content:
The UCC protocol lets a requestor contact a foreign host's logger and request creation of a process. The proposal maintains separate full-duplex pseudo-typewriter connections to the logger and the created process.

After the logger accepts the request and creates the process, that process establishes its control connection to the requestor. The RFC describes this sequence as an outline of a proposed UCC protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A requestor first communicates with the foreign host's logger. If the logger creates a process, that process establishes a separate control connection with the requestor.

references.text: Harslem, E. and J. Heafner, "More Comments on the Forthcoming Protocol", RFC 40, March 1970.
